## Background

### Last week: recap

Last week, we created scatterplots and conducted a correlation analyses using the three subscale scores (unintentional mind wandering, intentional mind wandering, meta-awareness of mind wandering) from the Brief Mind Wandering Three-factor Scale; a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens (Schubert et al., 2024). You can have a look at the questionnaire [here](files/week1/BMW-3_eng.pdf). 

**Reference**

Schubert, A.-L., Frischkorn, G. T., Sadus, K., Welhaf, M. S., Kane, M. J., & Rummel, J. (2024). The brief mind wandering three-factor scale (BMW-3). *Behavior Research Methods, 56*(8), 8720-8744. [https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02500-6](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02500-6){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

### **This week**

This week, we are going to work with data that we have generated (through simulations) based on data from a real project looking at how psychologists measure vocabulary knowledge.

Hanke Vermeiren and colleagues (Vermeiren et al., 2023) completed a series of studies to develop a vocabulary test for English-speaking university students. Among the tests they developed were measures of vocabulary knowledge (what you know about word meanings) and of reading experience (print exposure, based on recognition of author names).

**Reference**

Vermeiren, H., Vandendaele, A., \& Brysbaert, M. (2023). Validated tests for language research with university students whose native language is English: Tests of vocabulary, general knowledge, author recognition, and reading comprehension. *Behavior Research Methods*, 55(3), 1036–1068. [https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01856-x](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01856-x){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}. 

## Aims of the activity

We are going to:

1.  Download and organise your files
2.  Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
3.  Read in the data
4.  Build scatterplots with `geom_point()` and edit your code to change how the plot looks
5.  Calculate and interpret significance tests for correlation when you use `correlation()`.

#### Step 1: Download the files

To complete this lab activity you will need *four* files:

1.  We'll work with an example script called `4141_wk4_lab.qmd`. This is a Quarto document.
2.  We need data files called:

- `correlation-data-n030.csv`
- `correlation-data-n100.csv`
- `correlation-data-n1000.csv`

These files all hold scores on tests of vocabulary knowledge or of reading experience. 

- Different (simulated) participants' scores are on different rows of each spreadsheet.
- Different kinds of scores are in different columns of each spreadsheet.

Column names are shown at the top of the columns. The names encode information about what the column data are about in a `[..].[..].[..].[..]` four-part naming scheme:

- `[`what test? vocabulary or experience`].[`is r positive or negative or zero?`].[`is r large, medium, small in size?`].[`how big is the participant sample? small (30) medium (100) large (1000)`]`

::: {.callout-tip title="Actions"}
You can download the files from the handbook (see instructions under **Lab activity 2**). Usually they will be saved in your 'Downloads' folder.

Next, upload the zip-folder as it is to your Files space on the R-server: Look at bottom right quadrant of the R-server web window. There is no need to extract the files first.

Finally, open the example script by clicking on the file called `4141_wk4_lab.qmd` in the Files space on the R-server.
:::

## Step 4: Build a scatterplot

Now we are ready to create a scatterplot to visualise the relationship between two of the variables. We are going to look at the relationship between 'unintentional mind wandering' and 'meta-awareness of mind wandering'

The function we use for that (and for a lot of other plots you'll make for research methods and stats) is `ggplot()`. Inside the function we tell R which data to use and which variables to map onto the x-axis and the y-axis of the scatterplot.

> Action: Insert a new code chunk and use `ggplot()` to tell R what data to plot and which variables tot use. The 'unintentional mind wandering' score is stored in the variable `BMW3_UN`; we'll put that variable on the x-axis. The 'meta-awareness of mind wandering' score is stored in the variable `BMW3_ME`; we'll put that variable on the y-axis. Then, add layers to plot the datapoints (use `geom_point()`) and the line of best fit (use `geom_smooth(method="lm", se=TRUE)`).

::: {.callout-note title="Hint"}
## Hint

Use the function `ggplot()`. Start by writing `ggplot()` on the next line of the code chunk. Inside the `ggplot()` function, we need to tell R which data-frame (`data=`) and which variable to use (`mapping=aes(x= , y= ))`).

Then, we need to tell R what type of plot we want. We do this by adding a `+` to the line on which you've written `ggplot()`, then on the next line you add a 'geometric object', in this case `geom_point()`.

We also want to add a line of best fit. We do this by adding a `+` to the line on which you've written `geom_point()`, then on the next line you add another 'geometric object', in this case `geom_smooth()`. We want to specify what type of line of best fit, we do this by adding `method="lm", se=TRUE` inside the brackets of `geom_smooth()`.

This will give you a basic scatterplot. Revisit the lab activity code from week 1 to remind yourself how to change any of the features (such as the colour, the background, add titles to the axes etc.).
:::

The complete code chunk for the basic histogram should look like this:

```{r}
#| label: simple_scatterplot
ggplot(data = data_mw_subscales, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN, y = BMW3_ME)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=TRUE)
```

> Action: Make sure you've run the above code.

## Step 5: Run a correlation analysis

So far, we've visualised the data in a scatterplot.

> Action: Have a look at the scatterplot. Do you think the correlation between these two variables with be positive or negative? How large do you estimate the correlation to be?

The code below runs the correlation analysis.

> Action: Run the code below to calculate the descriptive statistics.

```{r}
#| label: correlation
results <- correlation(data = data_mw_subscales, # use the `correlation()` function and tell R what data to use
            select = c("BMW3_UN", "BMW3_ME"), # specify the variables we want to correlate using `select()`
            method = "pearson",               # specify which method to use; `"pearson"` is the default
            p_adjust = "none")                # we'll come back to this in a couple of weeks
```

> Action: After running the code above, have a look at the output. What is the value for r? Is it positive or negative? What does that mean? Can you describe the relationship between unintentional mind wandering in words along the lines of 'People who scored higher on ..., scored .... on ...'. Fill in the dots.
